transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-09 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Maya, Liam, Priya, Noah (Redwood) / Anna, Carlos, Sophie, Ibrahim (Peregrine)

Summary:
Peregrine is a mid-market legaltech company processing sensitive client docs; primary concerns: data residency for EU client matter data; legal-hold / e-discovery retention requirements; ability to do legal holds that may require cross-border access for litigation; guarantee subprocessor list and region pinning; BYOK/KMS custody and escrow questions. Redwood walked through routing policies, private/Dedicated options, audit logs, and escalation for legal requests. Agreed next steps and action items.

Topics:
- Region pinning and hard/soft affinity
- KMS BYOK + HSM options and escrow for e-discovery requirements
- Subprocessor inventory & contractual guarantees for data locality
- Audit log retention and e-discovery exportability
- Legal hold exception workflows and on-demand export for regulators

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, welcome. quick roll call?
[00:07] Anna (Peregrine): hi anna here, head of security.
[00:10] Carlos (CTO): Carlos, hey.
[00:12] Sophie (Legal): Sophie, legal.
[00:14] Ibrahim: Ibrahim, infra.
[00:16] Liam (Redwood SE): Liam from infra team, excited to dig into routing and kms.
[00:20] Maya: high level agenda: region pinning, kms/byok, subprocessor guarantees, audit logs & legal hold flow. we'll try to leave 10 min for Qs.

[00:35] Anna: to be blunt, our core requirement is we cannot have EU case data leave EEA unless there's a legal hold that explicitly requires cross-border access. even then we need documented approvals and an audit trail, like full chain of custody.
[00:47] Sophie: and our customers expect proof for audits — SOC2/ISO won't cut it alone, we need contractual guarantees and playbooks.

[01:01] Liam: makes sense. Redwood supports region affinity routing and region pinning. two modes: soft affinity (preferred region, may failover) and hard region lock (no cross-border processing permitted except via customer-approved exception). hard lock is available in Private and Dedicated, and for Hosted we can do strict region scoping for storage + processing but some subprocessors are global.

[01:30] Ibrahim: ok, what's the exact difference at the infra layer? does hard lock physically restrict model inference to GPUs in eu-west or is it a policy layer?

[01:40] Priya (SE): good question. it's layered: network and runtime policy ensure requests are routed to eu-region serving pool; storage and KV caches are pinned to the eu storage cluster. for Dedicated/Private we can disable cross-region failover. however, for hosted there are certian control-plane services that may be US-based (audit logs metadata index) — we can offer a private control plane for enterprise to keep control-plane metadata in-region.

[02:10] Carlos: that control-plane caveat is the biggie for us. legal wants metadata (timestamps, audit actions) in-region too. you mentioned private control plane can be deployed VPC on our infra?

[02:19] Noah (CSM): yes, the Private product provides a customer-managed control plane; we can do VPC only, or an on-prem bundle. that preserves audit log storage in-region and integrates with your ELK or SIEM.

[02:32] Anna: also, e-discovery: sometimes litigations require us to pull data into US counsel. will the system let us export a package with full keys, and how does that interact with KMS/BYOK?

[02:45] Liam: ok two things. first, export: we support data export workflows — you can run an export job that bundles documents + metadata + audit trail. second, KMS: we support BYOK where you provide keys via a supported KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK, Azure). if you use BYOK and retain keys in-region, we can require key unwrap to happen only in eu-region HSM if you choose. for e-discovery you might have to grant temporary key access — that's an operational step and we record it in audit logs.

[03:20] Sophie (Legal): temporary key access — that sounds like a governance nightmare. we need a documented process and proof that access was granted, who approved, and that the export job was performed. can you show us an example audit record?

[03:33] Priya: yes, audit logs include event type, actor, approval ticket id (if used), request headers, routing policy version, and the KMS key-id used. we can redact sensitive values but keep key-ids and approvals. retention configurable — default 90 days but enterprise plans up to 7 years.

[03:55] Carlos: default 90 days is not enough for us. legal retention might be 5-7 years. how do we store logs long-term without blowing cost?

[04:05] Liam: two patterns: long-term archival to your S3 (we can push to your bucket in-region) or send compressed logs to your SIEM. both preserve provenance. pricing for long-term retention is separate.

[04:20] Anna: what about subprocessors? we need a strict list with contractual guarantees that a given subset of subprocessors will not process eu-case data. many of your competitors have wildcard subcontractor clauses which vendors like us cannot accept.

[04:33] Maya: completely understood. we'll provide a redacted subprocessor inventory that indicates region and role. for hard region lock we'll limit processing to subprocessors physically in the EEA — e.g., AWS eu-west, GCP europe-west — and we can annotate fallback partners. we also can include an SLA clause to notify you 60 days prior to adding a new subprocessor affecting the region.

[05:00] Sophie: 60 days is good. can we get a contractual right to object?

[05:05] Maya: yes, for enterprise contracts we include a 30-60 day objection window and options for migration or termination in the event of unacceptable subprocessor changes.

[05:18] Ibrahim: technical edge case — what if a model shard or KV cache replication triggers cross-border traffic for performance reasons?

[05:25] Priya: we control shard placement; for Dedicated/Private we isolate caches to region. For hosted, we use prefix caching and we can disable cross-region cache replication for EU pinned projects. there are some third-party telemetry endpoints and health probes that touch control plane; those are documented and can be whitelisted.

[05:50] Carlos: can you run us through a mock legal-hold request? stepwise: legal files request -> infra performs export -> keys?

[06:00] Liam: sure. step 1: legal opens a ticket in your ticketing system and attaches court order. step 2: authorized approver (Sophie) grants export by creating an approval in Redwood's approval microservice (linked via SSO & ticket id). step 3: if BYOK is enabled, a temporary key unwrap is requested — that operation requires your KMS admin to approve in your KMS; all actions logged. step 4: export job runs within eu-region, bundling docs, metadata, console audit trail, and signed manifest. step 5: we push export bundle to your customer-controlled bucket or to a secure transfer link. we keep the signed manifest in-region and provide checksum for chain of custody.

[06:45] Anna: if the export target is in the US, that still constitutes cross-border transfer. we need to capture the legal basis and have it in the manifest, plus notice to affected customers depending on jurisdiction. can Redwood automatically attach the legal basis text?

[06:59] Priya: we can include a freeform field in the manifest for legal basis text and attach the approval ticket id. we don't adjudicate validity, we just record what was provided.

[07:15] Sophie: about SSO and RBAC: we use SAML + SCIM provisioning. can we have fine-grained roles so only a named legal admin can trigger exports? we also want MFA for export approval.

[07:26] Noah: yes SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning supported. Roles can be mapped to groups with least privilege. We also support step-up MFA via your identity provider for sensitive operations like export or key unwrapping.

[07:38] Carlos: we're also curious about how you handle eDiscovery search indexes — are they full-text stored in eu or do you use a managed search service that might live outside?

[07:46] Priya: search indexes for pinned projects live in-region; for hosted non-pinned projects we use a managed index with regional affinity. if you need total in-region residency, Dedicated/Private will guarantee index locality.

[08:00] Anna: any limitations on model variants? like small quantized variants that might only run on US nodes?

[08:09] Liam: right now model catalog has variants across regions. we can onboard a model variant into an EU-only serving pool as part of Dedicated onboarding. hosted has some limitations if a model isn't available in eu-region — we can provide a compatible variant or recommend pushing the model to a dedicated pool.

[08:28] Ibrahim: curious about subpoenas: if US authorities issue a subpoena to Redwood, what's the notification process?

[08:37] Maya: standard approach: Redwood notifies customer where legally permitted and if there's a gag we follow legal obligations, but we include notification terms in the DPA. for Private deployments you control the data and Redwood's obligations differ per contract. we'll share our transparency report and typical law-enforcement request flow.

[08:58] Carlos: okay practical ask: can you run a test scenario where we put a case in EU pinning and then run an intentional legalhold export to a US destination so we can validate the manifest and audit trail?

[09:09] Liam: yes we can run a simulated export on a redacted dataset; we'll produce the signed manifest and show the key unwrap approval flow. we'll run it in a staging Dedicated pool with EU pinning.

[09:20] Maya: we'll do that as part of the SE workshop. action: Liam to run simulation; Maya to share subprocessor inventory + SOC artifacts.

[09:30] Sophie: one more legal nuance — can Redwood include a clause that for any cross-border export required by law, Redwood will provide the manifest + export hash and only perform the transfer after a documented customer approval unless emergency order?

[09:44] Maya: we can agree that in the contract: standard notification plus a pause-and-notify clause subject to legal limitations.

[09:52] Anna: ok sounds promising. two smaller items: 1) retention of deleted docs for eDiscovery hold — do you have tombstone retention? 2) can you mark data as subject to legal hold so it is excluded from purges?

[10:03] Priya: yes. we support legal-hold flags at dataset and case level; they prevent background deletions. tombstones and soft-delete logic exist; retention windows are configurable and holds override deletions.

[10:20] Ibrahim: do you offer HSM-backed key escrow if we want a third-party escrow for long-term key custody?

[10:27] Liam: we have a key-escrow option via certified partners; we can integrate with an enterprise HSM or escrow provider so keys can be recovered under your governance. we can also do double-encryption where customer key wraps a Redwood key.

[10:45] Maya: ok let's recap next steps.

[10:47] Maya: Redwood will: 1) share redacted subprocessor matrix + SOC2/ISO assets by 2027-02-12; 2) schedule SE workshop for simulation during week of 2027-02-22; 3) produce sample audit manifest for the simulated export; 4) surface contractual language options for 30-60 day objection window.

[11:05] Carlos: Peregrine will: 1) provide redacted example of e-discovery use-case and list of jurisdictions where data must stay in-region by 2027-02-16; 2) prepare legal's list of must-have contract clauses.

[11:20] Sophie: thanks, please include the sample manifest fields in the deck.

[11:24] Maya: will do. any final q?
[11:28] Anna: no, thank you. good session.
[11:31] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts. meeting adjourned.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-heard acronyms (K M S transcribed as 'KMS' mostly correct), speaker overlap at 05:00-05:20.
